title: ATP Singles Ranking
text:
The ATP singles ranking is a point-based system that ranks men’s professional tennis players based on their performance in official singles tournaments over the preceding 52 weeks. A player’s best 19 tournament results determines their ranking, with points awarded based on the level of the tournament (e.g., Grand Slam, ATP Masters 1000, ATP 500, ATP 250, etc.) and how far a player advances. Points from tournaments are dropped after 52 weeks and replaced with current performances, meaning rankings can change weekly. Rankings are important for tournament eligibility and their seeding within the draw. The player with the highest number of points at the end of the year is crowned the year-end No. 1 player.

The “Big 3”—Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, and Roger Federer—have been dominating the ATP Tour for the past two decades, a testament to their consistent presence at the top of the singles rankings.

The visualization below illustrates the career trajectory for these players’ singles rankings, with circles denoting their Grand Slam victories at each point in time. Federer dominated the early years, particularly from 2005-2010, as shown by a cluster of green circles coinciding with his peak ranking. On the other hand, Nadal’s Grand Slam wins appear to be more evenly distributed across his career, without any distinct ‘domination’ period. Djokovic, meanwhile, seems to find his prime later than both Federer and Nadal, reflecting his later rise to the top and younger age compared to the other two.










The “New 2”—Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner—have risen to the top of the game in the last few years, bringing new faces to the men’s tennis landscape. Both have established themselves as standouts of the younger generation, challenging the dominance of older players.

The visualization below shows the ATP singles ranking trajectory for Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, with circles representing their Grand Slam wins. Alcaraz emerged as a frontrunner, rising to the top of the game slightly before Sinner, accumulating a few more Grand Slam titles during this time period. However, Sinner has recently surged ahead in the rankings, signaling the beginning of a fierce rivalry for the world No. 1 spot between these two rising stars.










Beyond visualizing the movement of these five players’ singles rankings over time, we can also examine the percentage of weeks each player has spent at the No. 1 spot throughout their career. The bar chart below highlights this data, showcasing how Djokovic has spent approximately 37.1% of his career as the world No. 1. This is evidence of his sustained dominance at the top of the game and consistency year after year, as rankings are a great data-driven measure of performance based on a player’s results against a variety of different opponents.

It is also interesting to note how Djokovic, Federer, and Nadal make up around 80% of the total weeks spent at No. 1 in their careers. This remarkable statistic not only underscores their individual dominance, but their role in defining modern men’s tennis.

text:
Header Level 2: Tips for linking/displaying figures and images.

Header Level 3: Linking to a Plot/Fig

Write you code to create your plot and save it. Save this script in src/figs. The source code does not need to be on the website.
Ensure that your plot is saved to figs/ by referencing the path with {here}.
At the top of the .qmd file for your page, add a code block that source()s the script that will generate the plot you wish displayed on that page.

For example:
source(here::here("figs", "point_mpg_by_wt.R"))`
Make sure to edit the code block so that the code runs only (no output).
NOTE: Code blocks that appear in .qmd files will call .R files only. Do NOT embed code blocks in your .qmd file(s) that will process data or create plots directly. Reserve .qmd files for website text, sourcing script files, and calling .png plot files. Developers and engineers compartmentalize project elements and do not combine all content into a single files. Doing so creates many problems not limited to code breaking and code-repair problems, Git merge problems, etc. You will follow a similar practice of breaking the project into pieces, save those files, and push them to the remote repository weekly for your team members.
This code-source()ing step also ensures that plot(s) are (re)created when Quarto rendering the website build files. You certainly want this feature so that new website elements and files are built during the rendering process. A full website re-build, however, is unnecessary when no element of the website changes other than the images and figures embedded within it. As a result, re-builds are not always necessary and will increase update time.

section: Header Level 2: (Optional) Circumventing a Full Website Build
text:
Header Level 2: (Optional) Circumventing a Full Website Build
Sometimes the main structure of your website is untouched but you have new data and you need to run a rebuild of your plots. Although re-rendering is not problematic, it might just take longer than you desire. If you don’t need to render the website and just want to build files, the following is a solution, though requires some extra work.
To avoid a full site rebuild (re-render) when you simply want to create and git push new plots:

Add your source()ing code to a separate file, for example, call_scripts/call_plot_scripts.qmd.
Add a code block to source individual .R files or all .R files in a directory.

Example:
#| include: false

# source a script file that this page depends on
source(here::here("figs", "point_mpg_by_wt.R"))

This .qmd file will render and create the .png files you need in your specified directory but the page will not be linked on your website. Technically, it will be visible at https://the_url/call_scripts/call_plot_scripts.html but this will be difficult to find. You can always remove the file or directory after rendering the website if you want to remove it completely.


Link the plot .png file in your .qmd file.

Homework #6: Lindsay Eisenman

Limitations associated with the below visualization:  - Only includes data from the years 2022-2025 and top 10 rankings  - Infrequent changes in the data result in flat sections in the graph  - Difficult to draw meaningful conclusions about performance from rankings 

Here is the code created to clean the Alcaraz and Sinner data:
cleaneddata_alcaraz <- cleaned_rankings_data %>%  mutate(dob = as.Date(as.character(dob), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(ranking_date = as.Date(as.character(ranking_date), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(height = as.numeric(height)) %>%  filter(name_last == “Alcaraz”) %>%  filter(name_first == “Carlos”) %>%  mutate(age = as.numeric((ranking_date - dob) / 365.25))  cleaneddata_alcaraz 
cleaneddata_sinner <- cleaned_rankings_data %>%  mutate(dob = as.Date(as.character(dob), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(ranking_date = as.Date(as.character(ranking_date), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(height = as.numeric(height)) %>%  filter(name_last == “Sinner”) %>%  filter(name_first == “Jannik”) %>%  mutate(age = as.numeric((ranking_date - dob) / 365.25))  cleaneddata_sinner 

Here is the code to create the visualization using the aboved cleaned data:
new2_ranking_timeline <- ggplot(mapping = aes(x = ranking_date, y = rank)) +  geom_line(data = cleaneddata_sinner, aes(color = “Sinner”)) +  geom_line(data = cleaneddata_alcaraz, aes(color = “Alcaraz”)) +  labs(x = “Date”, y = “Ranking (1 = Highest)”, color = “Player”,  title = “ATP Singles Ranking: Alcaraz vs Sinner (2022-2025)”) +  scale_color_manual(values = c(“Sinner” = “navy”,  “Alcaraz” = “orange”)) +  scale_x_date(limits = as.Date(c(“2022-01-01”, Sys.Date()))) +  scale_y_reverse(limits = c(10,1),  breaks = 10:1,  labels = scales::number_format(accuracy = 1)) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-01-28”), y = 4, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-01-28”), y = 4.25,  label = “Australian Open”,  size = 3) + #this adds a point and text to show the sinner’s AO win  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-09-6”), y = 1, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-09-6”), y = 1.25, label = “US Open”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2022-09-11”), y = 1, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2022-09-11”), y = 1.25,  label = “US Open”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2023-09-16”), y = 2, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2023-09-16”), y = 2.25,  label = “Wimbledon”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-06-09”), y = 2, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-06-09”), y = 2.25,  label = “French Open”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-07-14”), y = 3, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-07-14”), y = 3.25,  label = “Wimbledon”,  size = 3) +  theme_classic()  new2_ranking_timeline 






Plot 1





I used geom_line for this visualization because this is time-series data and I wanted to visualize the trendline and compare the rankings between both players.

Instead of geom_line, I could have also used geom_smooth what provides the following:   Advantages:  - Automatically fits and displays a trend line that reveal patterns in the data  - Reduces noise by summarizing trends instead of showing every fluctuation  - Good for data sets covering a large time frame  Disadvantages:  - Geom_smooth can oversimplify the data and obscure actual data variability  - Results depend on the chosen smoothing method, which can mislead interpretation 

Decorative elements of this visualization:  - Added bullet points on the trend lines to indicate grand slam wins by each player  - Since there were only 6 bullet points total, the graph did not become overcrowded  - However, if there were more grand slam wins, the graph would not be readable  - Another decorative element I could add would be a color gradient for the player’s age 

This visualization relates to Wilke’s “The principle of proportional ink” which emphasizes that the amount of “ink” should be related to the values the data represents. In this case, the lines are thin and trace the ranking movement per player, which is a good use of ink. However, the bullet points labeling each grand slam both players have won is a possible violation of this principle. Any more additional bullet points may lead to an overcrowded graph.

title: Key Directories
text:
Configuration Files
These configuration files are stored in the project root (.) directory:

.git: contains Git version control system files (do not delete)
.gitignore: specifies files and directories that Git should ignore (e.g, your .Renviron, .Rprofile, and other sensitive details) (do not delete)
.nojekyll: tells GitHub Pages not to use Jekyll to build the site
.quarto: for Quarto-specific configuration files.

The plot may feel stretched. If this is the case, you will want to determine good plot-saving settings for a website.
For example, controlling the plot saving parameter argument of ggplot::sggsave() using units = "px" (pixels) and specifying the width (in pixels) and height (in pixels) may be a good approach. You can determine what pixel dimensions would be good for a webpage by doing and Internet search.
Example:

width    = 1600
height   = 1100
units    = "px"
dpi      = 200 # or "retina"
